entry.title: Naming the replay record engine: the kind byte tells siblings apart
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be mostly the replay record engine plus loading-screen render and audio timing helpers, and 127 of them could be named. The reliable signal was the record constructor each emit function funnels into: every one stamps a kind tag at the start of the record, so sibling functions that look identical are told apart by that tag.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be mostly the replay record engine plus loading-screen render and audio timing helpers, and 127 of them could be named. The reliable signal was the record constructor each emit function funnels into: every one stamps a kind tag at the start of the record, so sibling functions that look identical are told apart by that tag.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of 150 unnamed consecutive functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function with a confidence level.

What was found

Verified The batch holds four groups: a family of about sixty replay record-emission functions continuing the previous batch, replay table and clip-state helpers including the load and save worker threads, a few loading-screen render functions, and a tail of timing-list and audio-spatial helpers.

Verified Every emission constructor stamps a kind tag byte at the start of its record. Decoding the first instructions of the unnamed constructors gave a kind map that separates otherwise identical siblings, including a particle-effects group that shares one kind with flag-bit sub-variants.

Verified Two inventory sizes are short: a handle-release function and a match-table search both run past their listed end. Both were named for their entry points.

Inferred The slot-ring machinery is treated as the replay clip recorder, following the previous naming batch: audio, physics and particle callers record their events into clips. An alternative reading, that the ring belongs to the audio engine itself, is left open.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the established replay prefix convention. Twenty-three functions were left empty at low confidence, mostly emits whose kind tag and caller give no event semantics. The next naming lane in this area should decode constructor kind tags first, before reading full disassembly.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the mapped executable image, resolve direct calls against the verified rewrites and lane names, scan all call sites for callers with an in-range check against the function inventory, and decode the first instructions of each unnamed record constructor to read its kind tag.

What was confusing or went wrong

Caller attribution by nearest inventory entry misattributes a few call sites to short neighbouring functions, confirming the previous lane's warning; every attribution was range-checked and the failures treated as unknown callers. The subsystem hint labels on the batch were wrong for the large majority of functions.

entry.title: Naming a 150-function batch: replay engine layout and two bad inventory entries
entry.summary: Most of this batch belongs to the replay record engine and the radio system, not the subsystems the inventory hints suggested, and two of the batch entries are not function entry points at all.
entry.content:
Most of this batch belongs to the replay record engine and the radio system, not the subsystems the inventory hints suggested, and two of the batch entries are not function entry points at all.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence for each name.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into five clusters: a radio station system at the start, script-native helpers, text drawing, script system and savegame upkeep, then a long run of replay record engine code.

Verified The replay engine has a recognizable layout: stream rings with tag-driven records, a generation-counted handle table, a slot ring with a cursor, a large dispatch table shared with effect updates, and locked record-emission helpers at the end.

Verified Two batch entries are not functions: one points at alignment padding plus a jump table, the other at a mid-function block that jumps back to its own loop. Several more entries cover two functions each, with the second one uninventoried.

Verified Five neighbouring tracker-removal functions are byte-identical except for one callee each, confirming the one-routine-instantiated-many-times pattern.

What was decided or recommended

  • 138 of 150 functions named, 14 at high confidence and 124 at medium; 12 left empty.
  • High confidence was kept for names anchored on strings, imports, verified rewrites or high-confidence callers; behaviour that was clear but worded by the lane stayed medium.
  • The coordinator should re-inventory the two bad entries and the uninventoried second functions hiding inside merged entries before production lanes take them.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each batch function from the memory-mapped image, resolve direct calls and string references, and scan every call site in the code section once to attribute callers. Read the short functions fully and the long ones from their heads plus caller and callee names, and check verified rewrite doc comments for what shared helpers do.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Caller attribution by nearest known symbol misattributes call sites that sit in unknown functions after a short batch function, so large offsets must be treated as unknown callers. The inventory subsystem hints were wrong for most of the batch and were ignored in favour of caller and callee evidence.

entry.title: One pose function verified; absolute reads into writable memory fail silently here
entry.summary: One medium task-system function was rewritten and verified first try, and its larger neighbour was deferred because it reads runtime tables through addresses the checker cannot serve. The surprise was how that failure looks on this machine: reads into the writable range return silent zeros instead of faulting loudly.
entry.content:
One medium task-system function was rewritten and verified first try, and its larger neighbour was deferred because it reads runtime tables through addresses the checker cannot serve. The surprise was how that failure looks on this machine: reads into the writable range return silent zeros instead of faulting loudly.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the checker, or defer with a precise reason.

What was found

Verified The smaller function fills one output record from a matrix and an indexed table entry: it calls a helper twice, resolves the entry table through two virtual calls with a fallback path, then evaluates a long straight-line sequence of single-precision operations. All 1200 trials agreed bit-exactly, both resolver branches ran, and a deliberately wrong version missing one store was caught by the heap comparison.

Verified The larger function reads a runtime-filled pointer table and several constants through absolute addresses the checker cannot serve, so it cannot be verified here. Its probe faults on every trial before completing anything.

Verified The failure looks different from the manual. Reads into the header and read-only ranges fault loudly with a note, as documented and as the checker's own negative control confirms. But reads into the writable-data range silently return zeros: four single trials with the table index pinned to different values all read zero and then faulted at the next instruction using it, and a rewrite-side read of the same place faults as designed. Only the original side sees the silent zeros.

What was decided or recommended

The smaller function ships as verified with no narrowed checks. The larger one is deferred as needing the missing shadow capability. Lanes probing similar functions should know a fault one instruction past the read is still this same gap, not a new one, and should be wary of any comparison that passes only because both sides read the same meaningless zeros.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane's rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows and run its two contracts with the lane's copy of the checker driver: the small contract passes over a thousand trials with a caught mutant, and the probe contract for the large function faults on the original side on every trial. Pinning the table index to several fixed values and re-running single trials shows the same zero read each time.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first probe used overlapping heap segments that clobbered a planted pointer and faulted before the interesting instruction; fixed offsets gave the true fault. The driver takes contract names from its own folder rather than file paths, which cost one failed invocation. A helper script named after a standard library module broke an import until renamed.

entry.title: Forty leaderboard slots verified, and two relocation lessons
entry.summary: A production batch of forty small leaderboard functions verified thirty-four for thirty-four on the stock checker, and the remaining six, which read a jump table through addresses with no relocation entries, verified too, because unrelocated reads currently succeed on this machine. Probe that case before deferring it.
entry.content:
A production batch of forty small leaderboard functions verified thirty-four for thirty-four on the stock checker, and the remaining six, which read a jump table through addresses with no relocation entries, verified too, because unrelocated reads currently succeed on this machine. Probe that case before deferring it.

What was asked

Rewrite forty neighbouring leaderboard virtual-slot functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the checker, one contract per function, at least one thousand trials each, plus one deliberately wrong version per function that must fail.

What was found

Verified The forty functions are six shapes repeated across seven leaderboard ids: an id check through a virtual slot that stamps an out slot, two key searches, one row fetch with no bounds check, one fetch-then-search, and one fetch-classify-switch. All forty passed twelve hundred trials with zero failures, none vacuous, every wrong version caught, no worker retries.

Verified The switch shape reads its jump table and jumps through entries that carry no relocation entries, which the brief lists as a defer case. It passed anyway: the guard window over the preferred base is unreserved on this machine and the reads return the right bytes, so the original executes correctly from the relocated image. Two separate checker runs agreed, and a case-swapped wrong version failed, so the comparison is genuine.

Verified The stamp shape stores a constant that looks like plain data but is an image address with a relocation entry: the original writes the relocated value, so a rewrite that hard-codes the constant fails whenever the worker maps away from the preferred base. The short probe passed only because that worker happened to map at the preferred base.

What was decided or recommended

  • All forty ship as verified, with the frame-pointer register skip recorded as each proof's only narrowing.
  • Do not defer unrelocated-address functions on sight; run a short probe first, and re-run them if the worker or host changes how the preferred-base window behaves.
  • Treat any constant that could be an image address as guilty until the relocation table says otherwise, and derive it with the checker's relocation helper.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble one member of each shape from the mapped executable image, generate one contract per function with a script that asserts each member's call sites and constants, build one rewrite crate, and run the checker driver once per small group. The wrong versions are second exports that differ in one behaviour each (skipped first element, wrong array, value plus one, swapped switch case, stamp plus one).

What was confusing or went wrong

The stamp shape passed its sixty-trial probe and failed the full run, which looked like flakiness until the first mismatch showed the original writing exactly the file constant plus the worker's relocation delta. The switch shape was triaged as uncheckable from the relocation table alone and would have been deferred without the probe that showed it passing. One progress-log timestamp was written from memory an hour off; every time since was read from the machine clock.

entry.title: Naming 150 functions: low-confidence symbol names that mislead, and a caller-scan trap
entry.summary: Most of this batch turned out not to be streaming code at all, and three of the low-confidence names attached to its callees were flatly wrong when checked against the disassembly. Treat low-confidence symbol names as no evidence until verified.
entry.content:
Most of this batch turned out not to be streaming code at all, and three of the low-confidence names attached to its callees were flatly wrong when checked against the disassembly. Treat low-confidence symbol names as no evidence until verified.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name and no rewriting or checker work.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into about nine groups in address order: radio interface drawing and station loading, spatial bucket-query walkers, one standard-library sort instantiation, area-clear pool probes, player slot handling, entity update and cleanup, draw-list accessors, and game-logic frame update code. Only two functions are genuinely streaming related.

Verified Three low-confidence names on frequently called helpers were wrong: a supposed radio-retune native is a player-figure field accessor, a supposed find-character native is a generic pool iterator, and a supposed radio-sprite renderer is a find-by-id list lookup. The wrong names would have poisoned every caller named from them.

Verified About fifteen functions call only into the encrypted first megabyte of code, where static disassembly is garbage, so they cannot be named from static analysis and were left empty.

Verified A byte-level scan for call instructions found callers for 130 of 150 functions, but cross-checking showed roughly eight percent false hits from call-opcode bytes inside other instructions, including two phantom callers on one player-slot function.

What was decided or recommended

105 of 150 functions were named, 7 at high confidence and 98 at medium, with 45 left empty. The next naming lane should distrust low-confidence native names in this address range, re-decode each caller-scan hit to remove false positives, and use field maps for game figures and players to pin down the accessor names left at low confidence.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each batch function from the memory-mapped image, resolve its direct calls against verified rewrites, lane names and merged symbols, collect referenced strings, scan the code section for callers at the byte level, and close-read the short functions plus one member of each near-identical family before naming.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first caller scan used linear disassembly and silently found nothing because decoding desynchronises; the byte-level scan fixed it. The subsystem label on the batch said streaming for nearly every function, which was misleading until the call graph showed radio, entity and game-logic groups instead. Shell output redirection wrote one drill file in an unexpected encoding, so later scripts wrote their own output files directly.

entry.title: Naming a mixed batch: cascade shadows, postfx, imposters, content slots, routes, radio
entry.summary: One batch of one hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to span six subsystems, and the strongest naming signals were virtual tables checked dword by dword, string references, and a full-text caller scan, in that order.
entry.content:
One batch of one hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to span six subsystems, and the strongest naming signals were virtual tables checked dword by dword, string references, and a full-text caller scan, in that order.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of one hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions, with a confidence level and one sentence of evidence each.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into cascade shadow code, a postfx class with constructor, destructor and factory, tree imposter rendering, downloadable content slot management, network route handling, and a radio display state machine with logo loading.

Verified Four inventory sizes swallow later entries; the true functions end at their return or jump instructions. Three real functions between batch entries appear in no list and should be claimed by the next lane.

Verified Code below a boundary early in the executable is encrypted on disk and decodes as garbage, so any name depending on those callees can rest only on call-site shape. Two low-confidence native labels in that area were disproved by reading their readable neighbors.

Inferred The radio display modes are plain numbers in a switch, so those names describe each case's effect rather than a mode meaning.

What was decided or recommended

One hundred forty-three functions were named, thirty-six at high confidence and the rest at medium. Seven were left empty: one unknown flag getter, two jump stubs, two dispatch thunks with unknown targets, and two thunks into the encrypted region. The next naming lane should verify virtual table slots directly before trusting slot labels, and should decode jump tables rather than treating switch cases as independent functions.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the memory-mapped image, resolve string and import references, scan the full text for direct callers, attribute each caller to its nearest known symbol, read the small functions completely, and check claimed virtual table slots against the read-only data section.

What was confusing or went wrong

Caller attribution by nearest symbol initially credited one short orchestrator with calls that physically sit past its padding; linear disassembly showed they belong to an unlisted neighbor function. Several lane-given caller names in the area describe unrelated behavior and were treated as context only.

entry.title: A callee slot called with two different arities, verified by fault parity
entry.summary: One rewrite in this batch is proven identical even though an eighth of its trials crash on both sides: the original calls one virtual slot first with an argument and later without, and the checker's fixed-pop stub pops the return address on the second call. Matching the crash exactly turned out to be the proof.
entry.content:
One rewrite in this batch is proven identical even though an eighth of its trials crash on both sides: the original calls one virtual slot first with an argument and later without, and the checker's fixed-pop stub pops the return address on the second call. Matching the crash exactly turned out to be the proof.

What was asked

Rewrite forty small task-system functions and prove each identical over a thousand trials, with one deliberately wrong version per function that must fail.

What was found

Verified Thirty-seven functions verified, three deferred, none unreached. Two findings stood out. First, a gated refresh routine invokes the same driver slot twice with different stack shapes: once with its object pushed, once with register only. Against the one-word callee the second call unbalances the stack, and both the original and the rewrite fault with the same code before the float copy that follows. A wrong version that balances the call survives and is caught, which shows the contract observes the behaviour. Second, an event constructor plants a vtable pointer off by exactly sixteen megabytes on the stock worker while mapping, relocation, patch and stub evidence all check out, so its provably correct rewrite waits on a worker fix.

What was decided or recommended

The refresh routine counts as verified with the unexecuted float copy listed as narrowing, and the constructor stays deferred with its rewrite kept for re-run. Lanes meeting a mixed-arity slot should reproduce the imbalance rather than route around it, and should re-decode with the recursive decoder before trusting triage reads.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts for the gated refresh routine: about an eighth of trials end fault against fault with identical codes while the rest compare fully, and the balanced-call wrong version fails on termination. The constructor's planted pointer differs from the correct value by a constant sixteen megabytes on every seed.

What was confusing or went wrong

Contract addresses are file addresses minus the image base while rewrites use absolute ones, and mixing the two faulted every trial until spotted. A per-trial pin cycle silently phase-locked with a gate so a whole path never ran, and probe runs kept overwriting the lane results file until it was rebuilt from the generator scripts.

entry.title: Production lane: the worker relocates absolute immediates, and data reads work without the shadow
entry.summary: A production batch of five task-system functions verified three of them and overturned two working assumptions about the checker: absolute immediates in executed code arrive relocated even though the executable carries no relocation entries for them, and unrelocated data reads observe true bytes with working fills and resets on this host.
entry.content:
A production batch of five task-system functions verified three of them and overturned two working assumptions about the checker: absolute immediates in executed code arrive relocated even though the executable carries no relocation entries for them, and unrelocated data reads observe true bytes with working fills and resets on this host.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring task-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the stock checker, at least one thousand trials each plus a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

  • Verified Three functions verified, twelve hundred trials each with zero failures: a small guarded queue routine with five callees including a virtual-table slot, a table scan with a scorer call and a frame-cookie check, and a large pure floating-point leaf with exact operation order.
  • Verified The worker relocates absolute immediates. A function returning a scan-end pointer produced a value differing from the file bytes by exactly the worker image delta, although the file has no relocation entries at those sites. Rewrites must pass such pointers through the relocated-address helper or call and return comparisons fail.
  • Verified Unrelocated data reads work on this host. Read-only constants came back with true file values, writable-global writes were visible through the globals check, planted values reached the original, and a one-hundred-five-trial probe showed no cross-trial contamination.
  • Verified Two narrowings worth knowing: one function reads an uninitialised stack slot for an output lane, and another pushes a flag dword whose upper bytes are never written; both were pinned with a zero stack fill on both sides and recorded as narrowed.
  • Verified A contract list of global values writes consecutive words, not per-trial cycles; per-trial cycling needs an explicit cycle entry. A corroborating detail: the inventory size of the large leaf is twenty-four bytes short of its true return address.

What was decided or recommended

  • Verify data-heavy functions on this worker instead of deferring them for the missing shadow; probe first, since reads, fills and resets all hold here.
  • Route every immediate-derived pointer through the relocated-address helper whenever it reaches a call argument or a return value.
  • Regenerate mutants in the same command as the build: editing a rewrite without regenerating briefly shipped a mutant that differed in two behaviours instead of one.
  • The two unreached functions (a deep dispatch routine and a large state machine) have full retry kits in the lane report: callee maps, plant needs and known cautions.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's three contracts with the stock worker and driver: each correct rewrite passes all trials with no failures and is not vacuous, and each wrong version fails on every trial that executes the omitted store. The relocation finding reproduces by comparing the scan-end return value against the file bytes: the difference equals the worker image delta exactly. The zeros-fill mutant analysis reproduces by checking which trials pass with the omission: exactly the trials whose fill makes every omitted store a no-op.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first triage concluded four of the five functions were unverifiable and was wrong; only a probe showing the original reading a true constant overturned it, which cost one rebuild cycle but saved the lane. A contract key placed at the wrong level and a word-versus-byte offset mix-up each cost one validation round. The stale-mutant episode above was the only real defect produced, and it was caught by reading the failure breakdown instead of the headline count.

entry.title: Five event-handler methods verified, one with a surprising register mix-up
entry.summary: All five methods in this production batch were rewritten in Rust and proven identical to the originals over at least a thousand trials each. The most interesting one reloads the wrong stack slot after pushing a value, so two calls and the stored result use a build answer where the code appears to use the saved subject. The rewrite reproduces that behaviour exactly.
entry.content:
All five methods in this production batch were rewritten in Rust and proven identical to the originals over at least a thousand trials each. The most interesting one reloads the wrong stack slot after pushing a value, so two calls and the stored result use a build answer where the code appears to use the saved subject. The rewrite reproduces that behaviour exactly.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring event-handler methods in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original using the project checker, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting states and compares return values, written memory, outgoing calls and faults.

What was found

Verified All five rewrites passed at least 1200 trials each with every outgoing call firing and a deliberately wrong version failing as required.

Verified One method's nonzero path contains a stack-slot mix-up: after pushing the helper object, the instruction that looks like a restore of the saved subject actually reads the slot holding the previous call's answer. Both follow-up calls and the stored response use that answer instead. The checker caught the first rewrite, which had assumed a clean restore, and the corrected rewrite matches.

Verified Three early exits in the largest method return whatever the caller happened to leave in a register. The contract pins that register to a fixed value so the exits are still checked on every trial.

Verified A float-entry gate reads "backwards" from how it looks: the compare instruction reports the reverse direction, so events are fresh when their time is positive, not negative. The first rewrite had it inverted and the checker showed the original exiting on trials where the rewrite proceeded.

What was decided or recommended

All five rewrites were accepted with their proofs. Two narrowings are disclosed with the results: one proof skips the stack comparison because the original reuses its own incoming argument slot as scratch, and the largest proof pins the incoming register and lists the deep side-branches its inputs never take. A later lane can widen those with longer input cycles; the report names the exact trials to align.

How to reproduce it

Each function has a contract file and a verdict file in the lane output folders. Regenerating a contract from its generator script and running the stock checker driver on it reproduces the pass, and the wrong-version export in each lane crate reproduces the required failure.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first relocation screen falsely reported that the batch reads unrelocated memory, because the script added a base value the library had already included. The float-gate inversion cost one probe cycle. Two argument counts were first read wrong (seven, not eight; four, not five) and were caught by recounting every call's pushes after an earlier function returned into garbage for the same reason. A duplicate include line from a retried shell command broke one build and briefly made a wrong-version run meaningless; it was rebuilt and rerun properly.

entry.title: Naming batch: text-case tail, font style records, cascade shadows
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions resolved into three clean groups: the tail of the game-text-to-unicode switch, the core of the font and text-style system, and render code for shader variables and cascade shadows. One hundred thirty-five received names, most at high or medium confidence, and fifteen were left unnamed where the role could not be determined.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive unnamed functions resolved into three clean groups: the tail of the game-text-to-unicode switch, the core of the font and text-style system, and render code for shader variables and cascade shadows. One hundred thirty-five received names, most at high or medium confidence, and fifteen were left unnamed where the role could not be determined.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence per name and no vague or address-based names.

What was found

Verified The first 52 functions are the final case bodies of the per-character game-text-to-unicode switch, each returning one mapped value, continuing the run two earlier lanes had established. Each is referenced exactly once, from its own slot in the dispatch table, and the slot arithmetic confirms the input codes continue the sequence without gaps.

Verified The middle of the batch is the font system, mislabelled as streaming in the inventory. It includes the font startup routine, the fonts data file parser, a reset routine that restores every text attribute default, and a family of small setters writing two 72-byte text-style records. The reset routine plus one field-consumer search identified nearly every field: colours, alpha, font id, scale, line-height multiplier, shadow and edge sizes, and several single-bit flags.

Verified The script text natives write a different, larger struct, so the C++ setters used by menus and the HUD were named from behaviour and callers rather than from native names.

Verified The end of the batch is render code. The queued draw commands carry exact class names in their runtime type records, which identified eight functions to the precise template class. The cascade-shadow render phase contributed its constructor, target setup, handle allocation and the large shadow-matrix computation, plus small matrix and bounds helpers.

Verified One inventory entry is not a function at all: it points into the middle of the unicode switch dispatch table.

What was decided or recommended

  • Next naming lanes facing queued draw commands should read the runtime type record just before each command table first: it names the exact class in minutes.
  • For families of tiny setters, read the reset routine that calls them all with defaults before reading any single setter.
  • Two phase slots were deliberately left unnamed because a class lane had verified the obvious reading (deleting destructor) is wrong; contradicting a verified finding to fill a name would be worse than an empty name.

How to reproduce it

Decode each function with a disassembler on the mapped image, resolve direct calls against the merged symbol, lane-name and verified-rewrite indexes, collect referenced strings, and scan the relocation table for data references. For the switch cases, assert each stub has exactly one reference in the dispatch table and check the slot arithmetic against the known input base. For command objects, read the mangled class name from the type descriptor behind each table pointer. Caller searches over the code section confirm which subsystem uses each setter family.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early byte-pattern scan for references found nothing because the references sit at unaligned offsets inside the dispatch table; switching to the relocation table found all of them at once. The merged name database picked up this lane's own fresh names within minutes via the coordinator tick, so a familiar-looking caller name briefly looked like independent confirmation before its timestamp gave it away. A syntax error from an invisible character in a generated script cost one round trip and was sidestepped with plain loops.

entry.title: Forty leaderboard functions verified, and unrelocated reads work after all
entry.summary: A batch of forty small leaderboard vtable functions verified at full scale, and the surprise was the seven I expected to defer: their switch tables sit behind unrelocated addresses the checker was supposed to fault on, yet every one passed with its mutant caught.
entry.content:
A batch of forty small leaderboard vtable functions verified at full scale, and the surprise was the seven I expected to defer: their switch tables sit behind unrelocated addresses the checker was supposed to fault on, yet every one passed with its mutant caught.

What was asked

Rewrite forty neighbouring leaderboard-info virtual functions in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with the checker, generating the rewrites and contracts from their shared shapes.

What was found

Verified The forty functions are six shapes repeated across leaderboard variants: an id-gated tag store, an index search, an unchecked item fetch, a size-class lookup through a five-way table, a reverse lookup with an unsigned bound, and a key-to-value mapped lookup with a signed bound. All forty passed twelve hundred trials each with no failures and no vacuous verdicts, and all forty deliberately wrong versions were caught.

Verified The tag stored by the id-gated shape carries a relocation entry, so the running original writes an adjusted value, not the file constant. The first attempt wrote the raw constant and failed on the heap comparison; writing it relocated fixed it.

Verified The seven size-class functions dispatch through jump tables reached by unrelocated addresses, which the checker manual says fault loudly, with the opt-in shadow unavailable on this machine. They did not fault: the worker holds none of the preferred-base window, yet the originals observably read the true tables, producing each table's exact mapping on every arm across hundreds of trials, and the swapped mutants failed. What maps the game bytes at the preferred base is still unknown; the worker source shows no second image mapping, no emulation in the fault handler, and no shadow.

What was decided or recommended

All forty count as verified on the stock checker with the table-read provenance flagged on each size-class result. Lanes should probe functions with unrelocated reads before deferring them: on this machine the reads may be served correctly, and a deferral without a probe would throw away verifiable functions. The unknown mapping deserves a worker-side investigation.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane generator to emit the contracts and rewrites, build the rewrite crate for 32-bit x86 into the lane build folder, and run the stock checker driver over the forty contracts at twelve hundred trials each. Every verdict passes and every mutant verdict fails.

What was confusing or went wrong

The tag-store failures looked like wrong rewrites until the heap comparison showed the original writing an adjusted value, which pointed at the relocation entry. The size-class passes looked like false accepts until the per-arm behaviour and the caught mutants proved the originals were reading genuine tables. Both findings came from trusting the checker's output over my expectations.

entry.title: Naming a run of character-map case stubs, and a phantom second table
entry.summary: A batch of 150 tiny unnamed functions turned out to be consecutive case bodies of the game text code mapper, each returning one mapped value, and all 150 were named with high confidence following the previous lane's convention.
entry.content:
A batch of 150 tiny unnamed functions turned out to be consecutive case bodies of the game text code mapper, each returning one mapped value, and all 150 were named with high confidence following the previous lane's convention.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions that mostly come from the same source files, working out what the group is about first.

What was found

  • Verified Every function in the batch returns a single constant and nothing else; the constants increase across the batch through the CJK range.
  • Verified The batch is one slice of a much larger family of over two thousand identical constant-returning stubs, all served by a single character-mapping switch through one jump table, with a companion function that maps whole strings in place.
  • Verified Each stub has exactly one reference in the whole program: its own slot in that jump table. The stubs are never called; the table jumps to them and their return goes back to the switch's caller.
  • Verified Every constant matched the mapping table inside the already verified rewrite of the owning function, which served as an independent check of all 150 names.

What was decided or recommended

Each stub is named after the game code it handles, continuing the previous lane's convention for the same family, with high confidence and the font subsystem. Later lanes meeting constant-returning families should assert the shape in a generator script and, where a verified rewrite with an embedded table exists, check every constant against it instead of reading members one by one.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, decode each batch member, scan the whole image for references to each address, and confirm the references form one consecutive run of jump-table slots. Dump the full switch mapping from the table and compare each constant with the mapping table in the verified rewrite of the owning function.

What was confusing or went wrong

The batch's references clustered in one tight spot that first looked like a second, separate pointer table with a few hundred entries. It was the tail of the same single large jump table: the giveaway was that the entries continued the same consecutive stub sequence on both sides of the cluster. Two small script bugs (a mistyped variable and a miscounted run index) each cost one rerun.

entry.title: Three traps from a network batch: a 14-count loop, shifted stack reads, garbage call arguments
entry.summary: A production batch of four network functions verified cleanly, but three of them each hid one trap that cost a checker cycle: a down-counter loop that runs one more time than it says, stack reads that land on different slots after a push, and call arguments taken from stack nobody wrote. All three are the kind of thing that reads correctly at speed and fails loudly under the checker.
entry.content:
A production batch of four network functions verified cleanly, but three of them each hid one trap that cost a checker cycle: a down-counter loop that runs one more time than it says, stack reads that land on different slots after a push, and call arguments taken from stack nobody wrote. All three are the kind of thing that reads correctly at speed and fails loudly under the checker.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring network functions in Rust and prove each identical to the original with the version 5 checker, one contract per function, at least a thousand trials each plus a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All four functions verified at 1200 trials each with wrong versions caught. The table below lists the traps.

TrapWhat it looked likeWhat it wasHow the checker showed it
Counter loopA loop set to thirteen iterationsThe exit test sits after the body, so the minus-one pass executes: fourteen table entries, and the snapshot tail proved itLast three snapshot words differed on every trial
Shifted readsStack reads at fixed offsetsPushes ahead of the reads move the frame, so two reads hit neighbouring slots: computed values landed where fill was expected and triple words shuffled by oneCall arguments plus-infinity versus not-a-number on the same trial
Garbage argumentAn ordinary forwarded valueOne forwarded slot is never written by the function, so the original passes whatever the stack held; the contract pins a known fill and the rewrite hard-codes it, declared as a narrowingNothing failed: found by auditing every read against every write, then confirmed by reference scan

Verified Direct calls into the encrypted first megabyte of code intercept normally; a function making four such calls ran all trials cleanly with them stubbed.

Inferred The four functions form one subsystem: the largest drives the state machine of another with constant arguments, which in turn calls the table builder of the batch for message rebuilds.

What was decided or recommended

  • Count down-counter loops from the exit test, not the load: if the test is at the bottom, the terminal pass runs.
  • Recompute every frame offset after each push in hand analysis; a flat read of a call setup is wrong whenever pushes precede addressed reads.
  • Audit every stack read against the write set before writing the rewrite; anything without a writer is fill (declare it) or a real defect (report it).

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the batch with capstone through the mapped image, decode the message-table init loop end to end, and trace the frame pointer through each multi-push call setup before assigning slots. Run each contract with a few dozen trials first: the snapshot and call-argument diffs point at the exact misunderstood word.

What was confusing or went wrong

The shifted reads bit twice: first as two swapped forwarded arguments, then as computed values mistaken for fill. Both times the guilty assumption felt certain until the checker diff showed two values that could not come from the same slot. The lesson held on the third function, whose similar setup was decoded correctly the first time.

entry.title: One menu step loops forever on some inputs
entry.summary: Verified A seventeen-way menu navigation step in the replay code never returns when its step delta is zero or a positive multiple of four: a skip loop keeps a value that is already one or two, and adding such a delta modulo four leaves it unchanged, so the loop has a fixed point. The differential proof therefore excludes multiples of four from that input; everything else about the function verified over twelve hundred trials.
entry.content:
Verified A seventeen-way menu navigation step in the replay code never returns when its step delta is zero or a positive multiple of four: a skip loop keeps a value that is already one or two, and adding such a delta modulo four leaves it unchanged, so the loop has a fixed point. The differential proof therefore excludes multiples of four from that input; everything else about the function verified over twelve hundred trials.

What was asked

Rewrite four neighbouring replay and menu functions in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with at least one thousand differential trials plus one deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All four verified first or after small fixes, each wrong version caught. Three findings are worth passing on. First, the hang above: one case of the largest function steps a small value modulo four in a loop that exits once the value leaves one and two. With a zero or positive-multiple-of-four delta the value never leaves, so the original spins forever. Negative multiples do not hang, because truncating division pushes the value out of the pair; they were excluded anyway as a conservative superset.

Verified Second, even-length script cycles parity-lock values to switch cases. With a twenty-long case rotation, a four-long flag cycle freezes each case to one flag value, so some branches can never fire; the symptom is callees that never fire no matter how many trials run. All cycles in the final contract use lengths coprime to the case rotation. Third, three shared callees had surprising conventions, settled by auditing stack balance across every call site: a placement call takes one stack argument with two leading words belonging to a later five-argument draw call, and a commit call cleans nothing.

What was decided or recommended

  • Exclude multiples of four from the stepper input and record the exclusion in the result row, with the hang probe as evidence, rather than weakening anything else.
  • Keep every pin and script cycle length coprime to the case rotation, and assert the co-primality in the contract generator.
  • When a multi-call sequence balances only with an odd cleanup, recount from function entry: a locally plausible convention can still drift the stack and corrupt the return.

How to reproduce it

Run the menu-step function with the skipping case selected, the head flag set, and a step delta of four: both the original and a faithful rewrite hit the trial watchdog. Replace the rewrite with any fast stand-in and the trial still takes the full watchdog, which attributes the hang to the original side. Separately, the modulo-four code shape used by the loop was brute-forced equal to a truncating remainder over three hundred thousand values including the extremes, with zero mismatches.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first probe of the largest function failed nearly every trial on the return value: almost every case returns whatever the last value-setting instruction left behind rather than a computed result, so each case needed its own return accounting, including one case where the answer register is reloaded midway. One flag-fixup condition was also read backwards (the heap diff showed a cleared byte where a kept one was expected). Both were found by reading single failing trials rather than the aggregate verdict.

entry.title: Naming a radar batch: a 2344-case switch, RTTI class names, and misnamed input slots
entry.summary: Most of this naming batch turned out to be radar and blip code, not input code, and two thirds of it turned out to be switch case bodies rather than functions at all.
entry.content:
Most of this naming batch turned out to be radar and blip code, not input code, and two thirds of it turned out to be switch case bodies rather than functions at all.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed functions in the input-ui cluster, working out what the group is about first and leaving anything unclear unnamed with low confidence.

What was found

Verified The batch splits in two. The first 56 entries are the radar and minimap subsystem: blip pool management, blip creation and renaming used by script natives, map tile streaming and drawing, radar projection math, and per-frame render workers. The remaining 94 entries are not functions: each is a six-byte case body returning one constant, and all belong to a single 2344-case character-to-unicode switch whose jump table points at every case in order.

Verified Compiler type records yielded exact class names for two font helper classes, including their constructors and per-line callbacks for counting lines and rendering text.

Verified The 1500-entry slot array in this code is the blip array, with fixed field offsets for colour, alpha, display mode, sprite, type, handle and flags, confirmed by reading the setter functions. Several nearby functions other lanes named as input slots operate on blip records instead.

Verified One inventory entry is a mid-function address with code flowing straight into it and an existing overlapping function, so it is not a real entry point and was left unnamed.

What was decided or recommended

  • Name the switch cases systematically after the dispatcher and case value, keeping the input-to-output mapping in the evidence, so the coordinator can either keep or drop them as a set.
  • Re-check names containing input slot near the blip code: any reader of the blip array belongs to radar.
  • Treat claims that inventory entries are not functions as needing an independent check, as usual.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble through the mapped executable image and decode one known function end to end before trusting the mapping. For each batch entry collect direct callees, data references, whole-image cross references, and names of enclosing caller functions from the merged symbol sets. Check runs of tiny identical functions for a shared jump table, and check data references landing just before a vtable for type records naming the class.

What was confusing or went wrong

The coarse cluster label said input-ui and several neighbour names said input slot, which pointed the wrong way until the blip field offsets settled it. One helper address carries a script-native name in the symbol set but behaves as the delete operator on every path examined. A first scan for cross references missed most of them because it skipped the code section, where the jump table lives; scanning the whole image fixed it.

entry.title: Naming batch 66: input, viewports, text, hud, settings
entry.summary: Named 141 of 150 consecutive functions across six areas: keyboard and pad input, the viewport manager, the styled text and brief system, hud elements and draw, and profile settings. The rest were single unexplained stores or calls into encrypted code.
entry.content:
Named 141 of 150 consecutive functions across six areas: keyboard and pad input, the viewport manager, the styled text and brief system, hud elements and draw, and profile settings. The rest were single unexplained stores or calls into encrypted code.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, with a confidence and one sentence of evidence each, working from strings, imports, known callers and callees, and neighbouring structure layouts.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into six groups: keyboard layout translation and pad polling with rumble control; a viewport manager with per-frame update, sorting and render-phase draw emission; hud colour loading; a large styled-text system built on two brief tables and timed print slots; hud element creation and per-type draw; and a profile settings list with save-slot load and store.

Verified Two inventory entries with size zero are real, called functions: one resets every print slot, the other releases a text row's object slots. One entry starts in the middle of a jump table; the real function starts a few dozen bytes later.

Verified One tiny float setter is genuinely a virtual-table slot of the on-foot ped movement-blend class, and the documented field at that offset is the move animation speed, so it names itself.

Inferred The brief-label resolver tries a platform-suffixed label variant before falling back to the raw label. The shared pad-effect helper fed by explosion, weather and audio paths is most likely the rumble trigger.

What was decided or recommended

79 names at high confidence, 62 at medium, 9 left empty at low. The next naming lane should distrust size-zero entries and mid-table starts, and check unnamed gap functions between batch entries, since several small helpers live there. Functions whose only evidence is a call into encrypted code should stay unnamed.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table per batch first: disassemble each function from the mapped image, record direct callees with looked-up names, import calls, referenced strings, raw caller counts, and data cross-references for virtual-table attribution. Read the short functions fully, probe unknown callees by entry disassembly, then name from the table.

What was confusing or went wrong

The raw caller scan reports false callers from call-opcode bytes inside other instructions, and enclosing-function attribution misfires where an inventory size overruns into the next function. Both needed manual discounting. Several shared helpers carry wrong native-mapping labels from symbol merging, so labels were only trusted when the code shape agreed.

entry.title: Two contract mistakes that pass quietly
entry.summary: Verified A transposed out-parameter script and a misread indirect call each produced a green verdict that proved less than it claimed; both were caught by checking variation shares and fault shares rather than the pass flag.
entry.content:
Verified A transposed out-parameter script and a misread indirect call each produced a green verdict that proved less than it claimed; both were caught by checking variation shares and fault shares rather than the pass flag.

What was asked

Rewrite six neighbouring audio voice functions in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with at least one thousand differential trials plus a deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified All six verified, with three findings worth passing on. First, the per-trial out-parameter matrix in a contract is indexed by trial first: each row holds that trial's words for every declared write. One row per write also validates and the run passes, but every trial then reuses the same first words, so scripted nulls and edge values never happen. The symptom is a healthy pass with a flat fault share where faults were designed in. Second, an indirect call reached by a single load from the object is a data-table call, not a virtual call: planting the stub behind an extra table makes the original read past the fabricated object into random fill and fault exactly on the trials where that call fires. The symptom is unmistakable once seen. Third, one helper call site in the largest function is provably dead: both words it compares are written from the same source with no writer between them, so the branch is evaluated every trial and the call never fires.

What was decided or recommended

  • Assert script shape in the generator: each out-parameter row must hold exactly one word per written word.
  • Check fault share and per-branch fire counts before trusting a pass, not just the pass flag.
  • Count the loads on every indirect call: one load means a field, two loads mean a table.
  • Note dead sites in the result row rather than deleting the branch from the rewrite.

How to reproduce it

Generate any contract with two scripted out-words, once with one row per trial and once with one row per write, and compare the observed out-word values across trials: the second form repeats two constant pairs. For the call shape, plant a stub behind a fabricated table for a single-load call and run: the original faults at a random address on exactly the firing trials.

What was confusing or went wrong

The manual's phrase for the out-parameter matrix reads naturally in both orientations, and the validator accepts both, so the transposed form looked correct until the missing faults gave it away. The single-load call looked like every virtual call around it; only the fault pattern forced a re-read of the operand chain. Both fixes were small once diagnosed: one rewrite plus one contract regeneration each.

entry.title: Naming batch 65: the texture store, user music, and three inventory quirks
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be six clean groups, and 132 of them now have names. The most useful signals were caller names and the verified rewrites' doc comments, not the code itself.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be six clean groups, and 132 of them now have names. The most useful signals were caller names and the verified rewrites' doc comments, not the code itself.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 unnamed functions in one address range, with a confidence and one sentence of evidence each.

What was found

Verified The range splits into a texture-dictionary streaming store with a dozen callbacks, a user-music folder scanner with its own thread, menu and loading-screen drawing, frontend audio players, sort helpers plus the pathfind node grid, and pad input handling.

Verified The music scanner skips nothing by accident: it tests file extensions against the shortcut extension and creates a shell-link object, so shortcuts in the music folder resolve to their targets.

Verified Three inventory entries are wrong: one entry points into the middle of the master audio update and is not a function, one entry listed with size zero holds real code with six callers, and one entry covers two jump stubs plus the head of the next function.

Inferred The texture store and the path store are registered through the same registrar with the same call shape, so the path store init could be named by analogy once the texture one was understood.

What was decided or recommended

Eighteen functions were left unnamed rather than guessed: mostly small setters whose fields have no known readers, and two jump thunks to unnamed targets. A boundaries lane should fix the three bad entries, and a class lane should confirm whether the path region global and the frontend audio block are class instances.

How to reproduce it

Build one evidence table first (imports, referenced strings, named callees, named callers per function), triage the whole batch into groups from that table, then read only the short functions and the ones the table leaves unclear. Caller names identified more functions than reading code did.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two callees sit in the encrypted first megabyte and decode as garbage, so the two chain-propagation names rest on the visible search logic only. One raw caller scan attributed hundreds of call sites to a single huge function, which needed a second look before it was believed.

entry.title: Naming the draw-command constructors and their draw methods
entry.summary: A batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be almost entirely the renderer draw-command system: 55 per-class constructors, 49 per-class draw methods, and the allocator and hash-table code they run on. 143 got names; 7 were left empty.
entry.content:
A batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be almost entirely the renderer draw-command system: 55 per-class constructors, 49 per-class draw methods, and the allocator and hash-table code they run on. 143 got names; 7 were left empty.

What was asked

Name 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, then naming each one with a confidence grade.

What was found

Verified Every constructor in the batch shares one unmistakable shape: it stamps the new object with the base-class vtable, mixes a per-object id against a global sequence counter, installs its own class vtable, stores its parameters, and returns the object. Each one references exactly two vtables, and the second vtable's type data names the class, so class attribution is exact, not guessed. An independent structure survey agreed on every class it had attributed.

Verified The fifty virtual methods the inventory calls slot one are the per-class draw routines. Each was read: sprite draws emit quads, state commands apply render state, light commands submit lights. The method word follows the one already-named sibling of the same hierarchy, which another lane called draw.

Verified The allocator is a two-buffer linear design: one function bump-allocates command memory with wraparound, one allocates data blocks that carry payloads, one flips the buffers each frame, and two small hash maps intern render ids with matching insert and lookup helpers.

Inferred Three small groups at the low end of the batch belong to other systems: streaming startup with its config-file parser, the loading-cycle tick, and a probe-record list used by camera code. Several inventory cluster labels across the batch disagree with what the code does.

What was decided or recommended

  • Name constructors after their vtable-derived class at high confidence once the two-vtable shape is asserted by script.
  • Name slot-one methods of this hierarchy draw at medium confidence, with per-function behaviour in the evidence.
  • Next naming lane: read the shared function inventory with its start key, not address, or caller attribution silently degrades to named functions only.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the mapped image, collect its call targets, imports, string and data references, resolve callee names against the merged, lane and verified name sets, resolve every referenced vtable to a class through its runtime type data, and scan the code section for direct callers. Assert the constructor shape per member before naming the family.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Three inventory entries are mis-split: one gapfill entry starts mid-data with two real functions inside its span, one size runs thousands of bytes past the next dozen entries, and one thunk entry hides two more entry points. The first megabyte of code is encrypted on disk, so anything calling into it had to be named from callers and readable code alone. A utility long labelled as a script-array native behaves exactly like a memory copy at every call site, and two audio-labelled helpers are called from light-drawing code, so both names are now suspect. A table of role-labelled counts is below.

GroupCountOutcome
Constructors55all named, high
Draw methods49all named, medium
Allocator, hash and frag helpers2423 named, 1 empty
Streaming, loading, probes2216 named, 6 empty

entry.title: Naming a save-system and menu batch: callers beat strings
entry.summary: A batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be the save system, the menu backend and a slice of player info. Naming 139 of them took one evidence table, full disassembly of the short functions, and two whole-program caller scans, and the scans resolved the hardest names.
entry.content:
A batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be the save system, the menu backend and a slice of player info. Naming 139 of them took one evidence table, full disassembly of the short functions, and two whole-program caller scans, and the scans resolved the hardest names.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name, confidence and subsystem for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first. No rewriting, only names.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into three clusters: about eighty save-system functions (slot scanning, async read/write workers, a block reader, failure dialogs, new-game setup), about forty menu-backend functions (a four-slot backend with create, draw, close and row, column and cell accessors) and a smaller player-info group (init, reset, control flags, control mode, score).

Verified The menu backend layout was mapped from its create, draw and close bodies plus the set-menu script natives: item count, column count, column widths, position, scales, selection, accepted index, accept status, scroll, colours, and per-row selectable, enabled and highlight flags.

Verified Two global bytes first read as menu-timing flags were re-identified from their callers: one is set by the pause-game script native and cleared by the unpause native, the other is read by audio fade, camera, depth-of-field and shader code during load scenes. A nearby float block belongs to load-scene timing, not menus.

Verified One player field is the score: the add-score script native calls its adder. The neighbouring field is probably money, read by the stats screen and the hud, but that stays an inference.

Verified Ten of the eleven unnamed entries are inventory mis-splits, not functions: jump tables, padding, a mid-function label, and jump aliases. Four entries with size zero are real functions and were named.

What was decided or recommended

  • Prefer lane-given names over stale merged placeholders when resolving callees, and prefer whole-program caller scans over strings for the uncertain cases.
  • Publish the menu-backend offset map as reference data so later lanes do not re-derive it.
  • Pre-flag entries that start with a jump, overlap a neighbour, or sit on a jump table, and mark the encrypted low megabyte off-limits in the inventory.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the executable's memory-mapped image and confirm the mapping against a second read path before trusting it. Build one table of calls, imports, strings and data references for the whole batch, disassemble the short functions fully, then scan the full code section once for callers of the uncertain targets and once for data references to the key globals.

What was confusing or went wrong

Short strings resolved from immediates pointing into code are false positives and had to be filtered to data sections. One merged script-native name contradicted a lane name for the same callee; call-site behaviour fitted the lane name. Two help-text helpers have no direct callers anywhere, so they are called indirectly or dead, which was noted rather than guessed at.

entry.title: A preset table verified, and a guard that holds nothing
entry.summary: One audio preset function was verified against over a thousand trials, and a probe of its four neighbours showed that the checker's safety net for absolute memory reads is completely ineffective on this machine: the guarded region holds zero of its several hundred blocks, so bad reads silently return unrelated memory instead of failing loudly.
entry.content:
One audio preset function was verified against over a thousand trials, and a probe of its four neighbours showed that the checker's safety net for absolute memory reads is completely ineffective on this machine: the guarded region holds zero of its several hundred blocks, so bad reads silently return unrelated memory instead of failing loudly.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of five neighbouring audio functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original, or defer with a precise reason and a retry plan.

What was found

  • Verified One function, a switch over six presets that programs parameter slots through a single two-argument call, was verified: all trials passed with every check enabled, and a deliberately wrong version was caught on all of its trials.
  • Verified The other four all read game data through absolute addresses that have no relocation entries, so they cannot run correctly under the checker on this machine. Short probes confirmed each one fails.
  • Verified The checker's guard for exactly these reads holds none of its region on this machine, on every worker process. Reads that should fail loudly instead return unrelated memory, and the original then runs on garbage and fails far from the real cause.
  • Verified Calls into the encrypted part of the program are intercepted without problems when they are direct calls; that was not the blocker for any function in this batch.

What was decided or recommended

The four data-reading functions were deferred with the reason that the read-only shadow they need is unavailable here, and the report keeps per-function retry kits with signatures, call shapes and the exact obstacle. Lanes seeing an original fail deep inside a function should suspect garbage from unguarded reads before suspecting their contract.

How to reproduce it

Run any checker contract on this machine and read the guarded-window coverage in the verdict features: held blocks over total blocks. Audit a function's absolute operands by testing each operand site, not its target, against the relocation table. Confirm a deferral with a short probe using a stub rewrite and patched call sites.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first relocation audit tested the wrong address and gave the right answer for the wrong reason; it was redone at the operand sites. A probe fault address first suggested the wrong function size until a wider decode showed the function takes ten arguments, not seven. The standard mutant run covers only a few trials, so the wrong version was also run as a dedicated contract for a full hundred.

entry.title: Naming a frontend, audio and text batch: caller scans lie, rewrites tell the truth
entry.summary: A batch of 150 engine support functions was named with 69 high and 72 medium confidence names and 9 left unnamed, and the two most useful sources were the verified rewrites' callee comments and full disassembly of the short functions.
entry.content:
A batch of 150 engine support functions was named with 69 high and 72 medium confidence names and 9 left unnamed, and the two most useful sources were the verified rewrites' callee comments and full disassembly of the short functions.

What was asked

Name 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence and one sentence of evidence for each.

What was found

  • Verified The batch is one address neighbourhood of engine support code: frontend menu backend and pages, settings load and store, audio engine init and update, a Windows Error Reporting crash submitter, file and settings path helpers, the GXT text manager, and save and load state machines.
  • Verified None of the 150 functions is reached through a virtual table, so every name is a plain function name with no class.
  • Verified Raw byte scans for call instructions report calls that do not exist when the marker byte sits inside another instruction; three caller attributions were disproven against true disassembly, leaving two functions unnamed.
  • Verified The inventory has wrong splits: one entry is a mid-function label, two entries sized zero are real large functions, one entry starts with garbage bytes, and one entry's range covers three functions.
  • Inferred The verified rewrites' comments about encrypted-region callees (file open, read, size, close) are the most reliable way to name code that cannot be disassembled from disk.

What was decided or recommended

Name each function from strings, imports, known callers and full disassembly of the short ones, and verify every single-caller claim against the caller's true instruction list before trusting it. Next naming lanes should mine the verified rewrites' callee comments first for any batch that calls into encrypted code.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's gather script over the batch list to build the evidence table of strings, imports, callees and callers, dump full disassembly of the short functions and unknown neighbours, then name from the table and validate the result against the batch addresses.

What was confusing or went wrong

The caller scan initially credited the async save driver with calls it never makes, which briefly misled two names until the driver's full disassembly disproved them. Several subsystem labels in the batch list were wrong (path code labelled as network code) and were reassigned from the bytes.

entry.title: Naming 150 audio and frontend functions: slot patterns worth reusing
entry.summary: Named 131 of 150 consecutive audio and frontend functions; the 19 left unnamed are bare field accesses, four large float kernels of unclear role, and one inventory entry that is not a function at all.
entry.content:
Named 131 of 150 consecutive audio and frontend functions; the 19 left unnamed are bare field accesses, four large float kernels of unclear role, and one inventory entry that is not a function at all.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names with confidence levels for a batch of 150 unnamed consecutive functions, working out what the group is about first. Only names, no rewrites.

What was found

Verified The batch splits into four groups: two sound-voice backend classes with near-identical twin methods, three sound-graph node classes with their tick helpers and trampolines, the DSP effect family with its platform backends and the voice render path, and the frontend menu and input code.

Verified Three slot patterns repeat across whole class families and can be reused directly by other naming lanes. In the effect family, the initialise slot runs a shared base setup then installs per-effect defaults, the refresh slot cycles an index and updates a parameter block, one slot is always a five-instruction address computation, and the advance slot rotates a table row then hands control to a linked stage. In the platform DSP backends the three slots are initialise, free buffers, and process samples. In sound-graph nodes the behaviour slot validates, binds operands, then creates a child.

Verified One inventory entry is a mis-split: its first bytes are a jump-table case belonging to the previous function, followed by padding, with the real code starting partway in. It was left unnamed with that evidence so no production lane treats the entry bytes as a body.

Inferred The small status queries on voice objects were named literally for what they test rather than for a guessed purpose such as playing or finished, and one single-call forward was left unnamed because play and stop read identically.

What was decided or recommended

Next naming lanes on nearby batches should expect the same twin structure: ADPCM voice methods mirror the plain ones at different field offsets, and the display-mode layout pickers repeat one code shape with different table ids. Caller addresses found by byte scan must be validated against the code section bounds, because identical byte patterns in data sections produce bogus callers.

How to reproduce it

All work used mapped reads of the executable through pefile, capstone disassembly, string and import cross-references, caller and vtable-pointer scans, the verified rewrite doc comments for overlapping addresses, and the audio class-layout tables. The scripts and the per-function evidence table stay in the lane scratch folder.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early version of the gather script indexed the memory-mapped image by file offset instead of by relative virtual address, which silently produced wrong pointer-reference addresses; a check decodes one known function end to end caught it before any naming used the data. Two large float kernels in the voice render path were left unnamed after their callers and callees still did not pin down their exact role.

entry.title: Merging the cloud review, and three traps on the way to checker version 5
entry.summary: A cloud session reviewed the repository for most of a day without the game's files and opened a pull request of 85 commits: trust tooling for the rewrites, checker version 5, the assembly of verified rewrites, the first crates of the lift, a shader translator, new site pages and a wider pipeline. The question was how to merge it under a swarm that commits every five minutes and whose lanes call the tracked checker driver directly. This entry records what was checked, what went wrong while checking, and what was decided.
entry.content:
A cloud session reviewed the repository for most of a day without the game's files and opened a pull request of 85 commits: trust tooling for the rewrites, checker version 5, the assembly of verified rewrites, the first crates of the lift, a shader translator, new site pages and a wider pipeline. The question was how to merge it under a swarm that commits every five minutes and whose lanes call the tracked checker driver directly. This entry records what was checked, what went wrong while checking, and what was decided.

QuestionFindingStatus
Does version 5 give the same verdicts as version 4 on this machine?Yes: all 38 existing proofs and all 34 wrong versions match the verdicts on record. Run twice, once from the branch and once from main after the merge.Verified
Do the new abilities work here?x87 entry values and state, vector arguments beyond the second, and snapshots of up to 64 words: their five proofs pass and their wrong versions are caught. The guard proof that is meant to fail does fail.Verified
Does the read-only shadow option work here?No. It needs the worker to hold the address range the original was linked for. In every 32-bit process on this machine (Windows on ARM64, running x86 code under emulation) a system mapping already holds that whole range before the worker's first instruction; the worker holds none of it. A fresh worker never helps, so the driver's retries cannot succeed.Verified (three fresh processes inspected, and the version 4 worker for comparison)
Is the guard still sound when the worker holds none of the range?On this machine, yes: the range is reserved and not readable, so an unrelocated read by the original faults, which is what the guard is for. That is a property of this machine, not something the worker ensured.Inferred from the guard proof failing with a fault on the original's side

Trap 1: a build that was not rebuilt

The branch was unpacked into a scratch folder from a git archive and built into its own output folder, so that nothing live was touched. The first regression then reported that the new proofs were missing from the proof library. The library was stale: an earlier, failed attempt had built the live tree's library into the same output folder, and files unpacked from an archive carry the time of the commit, which was older than that output. The build tool compares times, judged the library current and did not rebuild it. Cleaning the two crates and building again fixed it. A regression that had seemed to say "33 of 38 match, then a crash" was really a version 5 worker running a version 4 proof library. Rule: after unpacking sources from an archive into a build folder that has been used before, clean first.

Trap 2: "nothing changes for the lanes" was wrong

The plan was to merge and leave the live worker on version 4 until version 5 was proven. But lanes do not only run the worker: they run the tracked driver script and build their rewrites against the tracked runtime crate. A merge would have changed both under thirty running lanes while the worker stayed old. The first answer was a merge that held those files back; a trial of it broke the new ledger, which imports a new checker script. Before a second, narrower hold-back was needed, the problem went away for another reason (next section): with no lane running, the whole branch could be merged and the worker swapped in the same quiet window.

Trap 3: the quota ran out, and the supervisor did not notice

At 17:42 every lane ended within three minutes with the model service's "quota exhausted" error; the message gives the reset time. The supervisor saw free slots and kept starting two lanes a pass, each of which failed at once and took a batch of functions with it. Setting its target to zero did nothing, because it reads a zero as "not set"; the stop file did. Thirty-six lanes ended this way. Their batches, and those of older stopped lanes, are covered by the next finding.

A release step that never released
