Verified One heavily referenced getter is called from over a hundred sites and selects between the streamed fragment type and a stub. It is the single most connected function in the batch.

What was decided or recommended

  • Names follow the field strings and table roles found above; wording-only guesses stay at medium confidence and six functions stay unnamed.
  • A memory-copy routine carries a script-native name from an earlier lane and should be renamed; nearby constructor and destructor labels on the fragment archetype look swapped and need review.
  • Two inventory sizes are wrong: one function extends past its listed size into padding, and one entry overlaps the two functions after it. Later lanes should distrust sizes and re-derive them from control flow.
  • Caller attribution by nearest known function below fails badly in sparsely named regions, with offsets of several kilobytes. Attributions that far away should be treated as unknown.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped image only, never the raw file at a mapped address. Build one evidence table for the whole batch first: per-function calls resolved against the merged names, referenced strings, import calls, caller sites from a byte-level scan for direct calls, and virtual table references from data scans. Verify the mapping by decoding one known function end to end, then decode the short and unclear functions fully and read the raw virtual tables to confirm slot numbers.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two dozen functions had no direct callers and no table references, which first looked like dead code; they turned out to be callbacks passed as immediate arguments, found only by scanning for their immediate values. One pool routine is reached by a jump thunk, which a call-only scan also misses. Several callees sit in the encrypted code region and decode as garbage, so behaviour there had to come from callers and siblings instead. An early caller table misattributed one helper to a destructor; rechecking the raw call sites fixed it.

entry.title: Naming batch forty: task slot roles, shared code traps, and a misnamed constructor
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions got names, one hundred and forty five of them with useful confidence, and the batch paid for itself three times over: the three sub-task slots shared by every complex task now have project-backed meanings, five inventory sizes were caught overrunning their real functions, and a production-lane constructor name was shown to be wrong.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions got names, one hundred and forty five of them with useful confidence, and the batch paid for itself three times over: the three sub-task slots shared by every complex task now have project-backed meanings, five inventory sizes were caught overrunning their real functions, and a production-lane constructor name was shown to be wrong.

What was asked

Name one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions, mostly from the same source files: medic and fire tasks, cop and arrest tasks, ped data, render phases, interface markup parsing, radar blips, and the dispatch order system. Names only, no rewrites, each with a confidence and one sentence of evidence.

What was found

Verified The last three slots of every complex task form a first, next and control trio: the first-slot body never touches the current sub task and builds the initial one, the next-slot body reads the current sub task and picks the follow up, and the control-slot body drives the current sub task or just hands it back. This held for every complex class in the batch that overrides more than one of them, and two wander cases delegate to the base implementation outright.

Verified The current sub task lives eight bytes into the task object. That contradicts the drafted layout, which calls that field flags, so one of the two needs correcting.

Verified Five inventory sizes run past the real end of their functions, in one case deep into later batch entries, so a plain linear read invents calls that belong to neighbouring code. The affected entries are listed in the lane report for fixing.

Verified A constructor a production lane named as audio code is really a simple-task constructor: it calls the task base constructor and is used to build wander sub tasks. It needs a new name.

Inferred The radar blip names, the interface markup attribute pipeline and a family of hash tables form one data system: blip names are registered into a global table, config blocks are tokenised into attributes, and the attributes are applied to the same render state the markup code initialises.

Unknown Several read-only float constants decode as denormal numbers near zero while their bit patterns look like code addresses. One task slot that returns such a value was left unnamed because its meaning could not be established.

What was decided or recommended

  • Record the first, next and control slot roles in a shared slot table so future naming lanes stop re-deriving them.
  • Fix the five overrunning sizes and re-check anything whose evidence came from a linear sweep past an early return.
  • Adjudicate the two layout disputes (sub task pointer versus flags, pointer versus flag bit) and rename the misnamed constructor.
  • Keep three reliable shapes on file: pool allocation plus constructor means clone, an indirect call through the sub task means a type query, and a jump table full of constructors means a factory keyed by type id.

How to reproduce it

Open the lane scratch folder for this batch and read the evidence table, the annotated disassembly and the names file. Re-derive the trio by comparing which sub-task slots read the field eight bytes into the object and which only allocate. Re-check each overrun by decoding from the entry until the first return or tail jump and comparing the length with the inventory size.

What was confusing or went wrong

The batch list had to be re-read twice: two addresses remembered from the evidence output turned out not to be in the batch at all, and the near-identical layout of neighbouring task code makes this easy. Trust the batch file, not memory. The security-cookie slot also decodes as a plausible-looking string fragment and wasted a few minutes before it was recognised for what it is.

entry.title: Naming lane: browser layout, radar blips and task clones
entry.summary: One hundred fifty consecutive functions came apart into clean groups: an in-game web browser with stylesheet and table layout code, a radar and blip system with a tidy accessor family, viewport render methods, vehicle and ped factories, and task clone and destructor methods. 145 are named, 90 with high confidence.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions came apart into clean groups: an in-game web browser with stylesheet and table layout code, a radar and blip system with a tidy accessor family, viewport render methods, vehicle and ped factories, and task clone and destructor methods. 145 are named, 90 with high confidence.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence grade and one sentence of evidence each.

What was found

Verified The largest group is the in-game web browser: element parsing, style matching with hover rules, box layout, text measurement, and a full table section with column measurement, width distribution and row layout.

Verified The radar group is a family of tiny accessors over one blip record table, plus four draw routines selected by blip type from a per-frame update, and dedicated centre and north blips.

Verified Five viewport classes each override the same three methods: refresh, release and render, where render builds and attaches render phases. Four task slot-1 methods are clones and two slot-6 methods return urgency constants, confirmed by matching verified rewrites of the same slots.

Verified Three functions in the range are not in the inventory: a fifth blip draw routine, a radar update gate, and a small destructor-like function. Two listed sizes overlap their neighbours.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the existing project vocabulary for the same slots and structures, so later lanes can treat equal slots as equal methods. The unlisted functions and wrong sizes were reported for the inventory keepers. Five tiny virtual methods whose purpose nothing reveals were left unnamed rather than guessed.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the mapped image, collect its string references, called imports and named callees, and check claimed constructors and clones by the vtable address they stamp against the recovered class table list. Merged names from other lanes need a trust check first: one low-confidence native mapping turned out to be a player-position helper, and far-away caller attributions collapse into the nearest known symbol.

What was confusing or went wrong

Indexing the mapped executable image by file offset instead of address produced convincing but fake strings until a cross-check caught it, and the whole evidence table had to be rebuilt. A generic array allocator contains a resource-loading path that cannot be resolved without running the game, so it is named for its observable behaviour only.

entry.title: Naming cop tasks, html UI, event responses and frag physics
entry.summary: Verified A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive functions split into four clear groups, and seventy-four of them could be named from strings, callee names and vtable-slot semantics; the rest wait on the unnamed physics core and an event-id map.
entry.content:
Verified A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive functions split into four clear groups, and seventy-four of them could be named from strings, callee names and vtable-slot semantics; the rest wait on the unnamed physics core and an event-id map.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first, with a confidence of high, medium or low and an empty name where the behaviour is unclear.

What was found

Verified The batch holds four groups: ped task logic for police, search and movement-seek tasks; page layout and rendering callbacks; ped event responses; and fragment-physics virtuals with small math helpers.

GroupNamedLeft empty
Ped tasksmost, from task-pool and constructor calleessmall float and vector accessors whose property is unknown
Page UIlayout, vertex emission and callback invoke thunkscallback builders whose command cannot be tied to a type
Event responsesresponses pinned by strings or task constructorsthree slots gated on one unidentified event id
Frag physicssmall math helpers and a few pose solversmost virtuals, whose core callees are all unnamed

Verified Joining already-accepted names to inventory vtable evidence confirmed reusable task slot meanings: the first slot is the deleting destructor, the next is clone, then come the task-id getter, the abort check and, for simple tasks, the per-ped processing step. The three complex-task subtask-phase slots were deliberately not mapped to verbs because nothing in the project pins their order.

What was decided or recommended

  • Name the physics core helpers before more fragment slots, since over twenty virtuals depend on them.
  • Build an event-id map from event constructors so gated handler slots can be named.
  • Determine the subtask-phase slot order from the task executor, then rename the behaviour-specific task names to consistent verbs.
  • Keep the small float and vector task accessors empty until the underlying fields are identified.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address, and decode one known function end to end first. For each target, disassemble with capstone, resolve direct calls against the merged symbols, lane names, verified rewrites and inventory vtable labels, resolve indirect calls against the import table, and probe non-code immediates as strings. Join accepted names to inventory vtable slots to derive slot meanings, then verify every tiny function with a byte read, because disassembly windows that overrun a small function attribute neighbour bytes to it.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Two tiny predicates and one timer first appeared to reference strings and task-pool calls, but byte reads showed those bytes belong to the adjacent constructor; the evidence table was corrected. One inventory entry overlaps the next: a sixteen-byte guard was listed with a size covering the following function, so the two were treated as separate functions. One render-phase slot first looked like data in a wide disassembly window but turned out to be a real this-adjusting tail thunk, confirmed by its reference from a virtual table.

entry.title: Naming 150 functions: viewports, ped factory, HUD, loading, achievements, wanted
entry.summary: One hundred thirty-three of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names; the batch turned out to be six clean clusters (init and viewports, ped factory with its pools, HUD, loading screens, achievements, wanted level and blips), plus three inventory entries that are not functions at all.
entry.content:
One hundred thirty-three of one hundred fifty consecutive functions got descriptive names; the batch turned out to be six clean clusters (init and viewports, ped factory with its pools, HUD, loading screens, achievements, wanted level and blips), plus three inventory entries that are not functions at all.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive project-style name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, with a confidence of high, medium or low, leaving the name empty where the behaviour cannot be told. Only names: no rewriting, no checker.

What was found

Verified Three tiny viewport methods each return a short name string identifying their viewport type, and a nearby constructor installs the matching virtual table, which pins all four names.

Verified A ped-factory cluster creates game peds several ways (from a model, with weapons, the player ped, emergency-service task assignment), backed by six fixed-size pools whose dimensions were confirmed from the allocation code, with a matched allocator and destructor pair for the ped-data pool.

Verified The HUD cluster splits into one-time setup, per-frame updates for weapons, player status, timers and icons, and element creation through a single allocator; the loading cluster splits into begin, render, art selection, text panels, finish, and settings save.

Verified An achievement family of seven functions shares one check-then-unlock shape with a distinct achievement id each, confirmed by constants and by stat-system callers.

Verified The wanted cluster keeps thirty radar-blip slots per player with assign, detach, allocate, sweep and label-lookup helpers, plus a two-part wanted manager and search update.

Verified Three entries are not functions: two are mid-function offsets and one is a five-byte crash stub. Two more entries are tiny jump stubs aliasing real functions, and one listed size swallows the following function. Three existing hints or names were found wrong: a data-file hint with no referrer, dispatch-order hints on what is actually a HUD label table, and three lane-given native names that turned out to be the local-player vehicle getter, a wanted-level getter, and the C library random function.

What was decided or recommended

Names follow the observed evidence strength: class-qualified names where a virtual table pins the class, plain behaviour names elsewhere, and empty names with stated reasons for the seventeen unclear cases (four shared task forwarders whose slots are undocumented, six tiny predicates, two stubs, three non-entries, and two opaque helpers). The next naming lane should re-check any inventory hint before trusting it, decode every stub-sized entry before naming it, and treat the first megabyte of code as encrypted and unreadable on disk.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, never the raw file at a mapped address, and confirm the mapping by decoding one known function end to end. Then build one evidence table for the whole batch (callees with resolved names, imports, string operands), scan the code section for direct callers, scan data sections for virtual-table references, dump the relevant virtual tables to confirm class membership, and read the short functions in full while diffing twin families instead of reading each member.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two display bugs wasted a round trip: caller and reference tables keyed by lowercase address silently missed lookups done with uppercase, and looked empty until the case was fixed. A first draft of the name file assigned names to shifted addresses after a manual slip; it was thrown away and regenerated by a script that zips names to the batch list and asserts alignment. Several heavily reused helpers sit in the encrypted region and decode as garbage, so the functions calling them could only be named from their call patterns.

entry.title: A whole leaderboard family verified, and a checker anomaly that only fails on mismatch
entry.summary: A batch of forty small leaderboard functions turned out to be one template family in seven shapes, and thirty-three of them verified first try from a single generator, while the seventh shape exposed a deterministic checker-side anomaly worth knowing about.
entry.content:
A batch of forty small leaderboard functions turned out to be one template family in seven shapes, and thirty-three of them verified first try from a single generator, while the seventh shape exposed a deterministic checker-side anomaly worth knowing about.

What was asked

Rewrite forty small neighbouring game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the version four checker, generating one contract per function and one deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified The batch collapses into seven byte-uniform shapes: six table-lookup and rank-classify shapes that call one scripted fetch routine and differ only in a leaderboard index constant, plus one key-check shape that calls through an object function table and publishes a per-instance tag.

Verified Thirty-three functions passed twelve hundred trials each with every wrong version caught. Two genuine misunderstandings were caught along the way: the key-check shape returns the out-pointer rather than the key on a match, and its stored tag is an image address that must be relocated at run time.

Verified The key-check shape cannot be verified on the stock checker: the original side returns zero with the zero flag set whenever the scripted key differs from the expected key, and behaves perfectly whenever they are equal. Minimal all-fixed ten-trial contracts reproduce this exactly, on two separate instances, while the stock indirect-call controls pass.

What was decided or recommended

The seven key-check functions were deferred with the anomaly documented, keeping their rewrites and contracts for re-run. Proving only the matching path and calling that verified would have inverted the function under test, so it was recorded as not proven instead. A checker-debug lane can reproduce the failure in about a second from the kept minimal contracts.

How to reproduce it

Generate one contract per shape with scripted fetch answers covering success, failure, empty tables, present and absent keys, and run twelve hundred trials per function with a one-behaviour wrong version each. The anomaly reproduces with a single fixed script answer and a fixed differing expected key.

What was confusing or went wrong

The anomaly consumed most of the lane because every obvious cause checked out: the contract matches the passing controls structurally, the worker applies identical setup to both sides by construction, and the rewrite side of the same trials behaves correctly. The trigger turned out to be pure value inequality, which no mechanism in the harness should depend on. Parking it after isolating a minimal repro, rather than continuing to theorise, is what saved the other thirty-three functions.
